utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, quickly, because I'm tight for time. Your Honours will recall a somewhat heated, maybe acrimonious, argument about the admission of a document yesterday, which is on our list as number five, and had been given the -- what was the old 65 ter number of 1976. Owing to the eagle eye of Mr. Hannis, I have to say, we discovered that the document is, in fact, admitted. It is a different version of it. Therefore, it has different ERN numbers, and it does not contain the letter that was attached to the document from General Kukanjac. It is, in fact, admitted as P1295.16, as part of a 65 ter [sic] package for ST-183. Now, Your Honours, there is -- as I say, there's that difference because the original exhibit doesn't contain the letter, and this one does. So what our suggestion is, is that we should replace what was the document that is admitted as P1295.16 with this one so that the full document with the letter is there. Otherwise, we've got admitted two documents -- two identical documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do the Defence -- does either of Defence counsel have any views on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour. Ms. Korner explained to us the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So the order is as Ms. Korner has cast it, that is, the substitution of the complete document for the one that's already exhibited. And if there are no other matters, would the usher please conduct the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we continue, could we have the 65 ter number for this document, please, for the -- so the record is clear. The new document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the one that we produced yesterday or the -- the earlier one that was already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The new one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The new one was given, on our list, 65 ter 1976.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: General, good afternoon to you. Before Ms. Korner continues, I remind you of your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, can I just say this: I have limited time left with you and I have a lot to get through, so I would be very grateful if you could literally answer the question I ask without any further detail, unless you feel it's absolutely necessary. Now, we're looking at the events which led to the formation of the VRS through the documents that were brought into existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we now have a look, please, on the screen at a document which has been given the 65 ter number -- oh, no, actually, sorry, one more -- document 1D175. Oh, which is document 7 in our list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, General, this document does not appear in your bibliography, nor was it in the list provided by the Defence, so I take it you've not seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't get the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. It is, in fact, the order, or the conclusions, of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted at the meeting held on the 5th of April to mobilise certain TO units. And do you appreciate that that came after the events that we looked at yesterday through the documents in Bijeljina? And, equally, do you see that it's in accordance with Article 107 of the All People's Defence, the one you discussed with Mr. Cvijetic? So the government is exercising its powers to use the TO to maintain law and order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm trying to see if it is, indeed, the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that's involved here. But I'm not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not. I'm sorry. It's the -- it's the -- if I can put it that way, maybe somewhat controversially, the proper government, the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as you put it in your report, the rump?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document adopted by the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct. I believe it says so at the top. Although it's not very clear. And it's signed by Mr. Doko.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look at the second page, please, in B/C/S. Actually, it's probably the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you were still in Bosnia at the time. Do you recall this part mobilisation under Article 107?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time; specifically in Bihac. I am aware that activities such as this one took place at the time in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you accept that this was a response to what had been happening, first of all, in Bijeljina and some other places, and also in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, can we move to the next document, please, which is document at -- the number is 20247; 65 ter number. It's at 8A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the duty operations team of the 2nd Military District, providing a report for the General Staff. Do you agree, looking at the head?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's dated the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to the second page, paragraph 3, in English -- in English, because it appears -- that page ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The situation in the territory. "The situation is becoming increasingly troubled and is reaching boiling point. ... it's deteriorating in trouble spots, especially in Visegrad, Zvornik, Jajce and Sarajevo. "Propaganda activity and charges laid against the JNA as the main guilty party for the recent events are continuing. Hatred of the JNA among the Muslim and Croatian population is becoming ever greater. The president of Bosnia [sic] claims that the JNA is the only force capable of acting to save the Muslim population in the Zvornik sector but is unwilling to do so, which will only compound further the hostile stance of the Muslim population towards the JNA." And that's right, isn't it, General: The JNA, again, stood by while attacks were launched in Zvornik against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wasn't there at the time, but, I repeat: It wasn't the JNA that arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina but only some parts of units. The army was breaking up all the way from Slovenia across Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was in the process of breaking up. Therefore, I can't really say. But if that's what the document says, I don't know what else it says. I don't know the context of the document in its entirety. Is this merely a report of the President's words, or is this something that he really means? And by "he," I mean the operative officer who signed this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, again, you see, you obviously didn't see this report. Do you think it might have been useful to you in arriving at your conclusions and evidence if you'd seen this report? And I'm going to show you one other part of it, and also we'll give you a copy to read over the break, if you'd like to. But can we look at the other part and then I'll ask you again the question I just asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at page 5 in English, and in B/C/S at page -- it's the third page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The previous page talked about the 17th Corps, which was the corps that we saw yesterday in Bijeljina. And do you see the words "the situation in the corps's zone is becoming extremely troubled and is most critical in Zvornik and Visegrad zones. Serbian paramilitary formations are holding more than 3.000 Muslim citizens in the Kula sector, Zvornik, under an ultimatum"? Were you aware of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm looking at this segment of the document and I believe this man, this commander, whoever signed the document, would like to see a position taken, would like to see a decision taken, would like to see steps taken. What I'm telling you is, at the time, the federal leadership included representatives of all the republics and all the nations. They were taking certain decisions. I know full well how this worked at the time, and what was happening. As far as I can tell, this person wants a specific position. He wants to know what he is expected to do and what task or assignment he will be given.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I absolutely agree. And, in fact, if we look at the last page, you will see that it's signed by a Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page in B/C/S and English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have met him, Ms. Korner, but I can't remember now. The family name rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. The reason I'm showing you this document is because doesn't it show, as I have been suggesting, that the JNA, contrary to what you suggest, that it was an independent above-politics army, was, in fact, by this stage, in 1992, firmly and completely on the side of the Serbs? And by "JNA," I mean the leadership, obviously.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the JNA was subordinated to the political leadership, comprising six presidents of the republics and two from the autonomous provinces. They all belonged to different ethnic groups, and they were obstructing the JNA in performing its tasks. On a personal level, I'm happy to agree with you that the JNA failed in its mission, and that's why the country that it was expected to protect eventually broke apart. Take my word for it. I know better than you how exactly the country fell apart, and I certainly know how the JNA itself fell apart.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, you see, it goes back also to what you said, that the JNA's role was to prevent interethnic conflict. In fact, in reality, it did no such thing, did it? Certainly not by the beginning -- not by March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that was the information we had at the time. Yet I'm telling you, we were under siege. Substantial forces of the JNA were under siege, being blocked by the paramilitary units. Whole barracks under siege. Flats and residential buildings where military families lived were under siege. These commanders were the people who were supposed to take the relevant decisions and they were under an enormous amount of pressure. They didn't know what to do. They were receiving threats. If they did anything, their whole families would be wiped out. It was a very difficult situation, and it was a very difficult situation for the then-federal state to handle. It was a no-holds-barred situation. Any method was a legitimate one. I didn't specifically analyse that, Ms. Korner. I hadn't realized that it was something that was at stake in this case. I am, needless to say, perfectly willing to take it up. That would, however, require a team of experts, including the Croat military personnel, Macedonian, Bosnian, Serbian. We should put together a tame of military experts from back then to draw up a thorough analysis of what exactly happened, but we might as well leave it to history and see what researchers in the future have to say about all these developments and what their judgement will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, can I say, on that last point, I'm not blaming you. I appreciate that you were under-instructed and you were not allowed or given access to a lot of these documents, so I'm not blaming you for this. I'm merely asking you whether if you had a look at this and other relevant documents you might not have asserted that the JNA's role was to prevent interethnic conflict.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I wouldn't change anything. One thing is certain, the JNA failed to do its job; I agree with that. But I'm telling you about what its role was at the time, what its purpose was. The purpose being to preserve the country. And, I do apologise, to stop the country from being broken up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It was to preserve the country, as we've already looked at, from what was perceived was going to be an outside enemy. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Ms. Korner. Primarily. All of the doctrine envisaged that as being the primary task of the JNA. And that is why it failed to find its feet, as it were, given what the conditions were at the time. The army commanders were Slovenes, Croats, Serbs, depending. Just to avoid going into the whole history behind this, how it all started back in the 1970s. They started grouping and regrouping the JNA officers within the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. I say that we can't go back to the 1970s. And, of course, your own counsel has a chance to re-examine you on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask that this document be admitted for the purposes to which I put to him, that his assertions about the JNA being there to prevent interethnic conflict, and not -- being Serbs [indiscernible] is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I don't think this is relevant. If we look at this document, apart from Ms. Korner's speech, apart from her interpretation, we find none of the assertions that are supposed to back the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And it seems to me, Ms. Korner, that the witness has accepted your underlying suggestion that the purpose of the -- the original purpose, let me put it that way, of the JNA had been improperly hijacked by the political directorates, plural, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My suggestion is by its own leadership as well, Your Honour, not just the political.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is admitted and marked. The -- I wouldn't say that Judge Hall enters a dissent. I have reservations. But by a majority, certainly, the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, very quickly, can we look at one more document on this particular theme. It's 8-- sorry. 8C. 20245. And it's 8C in our list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the 17th Corps again on the 11th of April. Its a daily report to the 2nd Military District. And if we just look, please, at the end of paragraph 2: [As read] "Spreading of war in the territory which brings anxiety among the active servicemen and citizens and pervasive fear for their families. Some senior officers from the 92nd Motor Brigade," I believe that is, "openly accused the JNA for not intervening in Bijeljina and Zvornik, not to mention the ban imposed to the same unit to intervene in Bosanski Brod." And that it makes clear, does it not, beyond a paradventure, General, that although many officers or some senior officers certainly were against it, the JNA were told not to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there is a -- there is a wrong translation. The part where it says "not to mention the ban imposed ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we -- can we -- could the General read out --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the Serbian and then we'll get the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you read out, please, General, from the screen the part that begins: "Some senior officers ..." And could you read that slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading, Ms. Korner: "A number of officers from the 92nd Motorised Brigade are openly condemning the JNA for not having intervened in Bijeljina and Zvornik, but they do not mention a ban on the intervention of the same sort in Bosanski Brod."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So if I understand that correctly, the writer of this report is saying that these officers have not mentioned the ban on an intervention taking place in Bosanski Brod. I hope I've understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Korner, it is very difficult for me to comment what the author wanted to say. He's not specifying which officers he had in mind, what their ethnicity was, what they were condemning or banning. Those were probably daily comments that were made in a barracks or at a position; therefore, it is very difficult to say something definitely. However, what I can say, and what I know from experience, we were all waiting for some sort of decision or assignment from the top leadership that would allow us to intervene or do anything at all. More often than not, those decisions were just advance, stop, advance, stop. Which was devastating for the army and which was conducive to its breakup, which was precipitated, in my view, deliberately and by design.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look at two other parts of this document, please. At the bottom of the page in English, the paragraph that begins: [As read] "Corps commander visited the area of Zvornik after which the corps command issued an announcement or an appeal to all the citizens to return from the places which they had moved out because the army guarantees them security. The announcement was broadcast by Tuzla radio. At the same time, another announcements" --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the second page in English. I believe it's still the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... by religious officials to the population of Zvornik and the surrounding villages about endangered conditions therein appeals for help against the genocide." And so on. And that's been broadcast as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we, then, please, to the next page -- oh, sorry, in B/C/S. Same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item number 7: "The security situation is without particular problems. A truck of weaponry was handed over to the SDS party Crisis Staff in the villages of Kozluk and Gornji Sepak. No killings and shootings reported. SDS is keeping the villages under blockade until they surrender the rest of the weaponry." And then there are rumours. So do you understand that, General - and I take it, of course, you haven't seen this before - to mean that the JNA, Major-General Savo Jankovic, who signed this report, has handed over weaponry to the SDS Crisis Staff in these villages?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. However, I don't know why they were given this, whether they were threatened or something else was at stake, but this is what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry to keep harping on this, General. But isn't it absolutely clear beyond a paradventure that the SDS -- sorry, the JNA was taking sides even in the absence of any clear direction from either the political leadership or its own leadership?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it is impossible to make such an assertion on the basis of these two or three documents alone. The weapons were distributed and seized, and these are the facts. I have to mention an example when the commander of the Varazdin Corps surrendered in Croatia and left behind hundreds of state-of-the-art M84 tanks in order to save his men. That was the ultimatum that he succumbed to. So there was total chaos that was happening at the time. I do know that the JNA was not only on the side of the Serbian people. They saved thousands and hundreds of thousands members of other ethnic groups by receiving them in the barracks, providing them food, and protecting them from various paramilitaries. It is not my intention to defend the JNA here. This is not my role here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, let's, just briefly, the conclusion of this document, where they say that: [As read] "Tensions in the interethnic relations ... in the corps' area of responsibility could result in open conflict. The most difficult situation is in the area of Zvornik because there are a large number of refugees coming to Tuzla and surrounding municipalities." And then this: "Corps units have been engaged in preventing the interethnic conflicts."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, very quickly, can I ask that this be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, once again, I object, because what Ms. Korner is trying to prove by this document is not contained in the document. That's the essence of my objection. Why? Look at paragraph 7, for example. Ms. Korner is interpreting this paragraph. This is not about the surrender of -- or, rather, the handing over of weapons to the SDS but rather it's about disarming other citizens by the SDS. And the gist of my objection is that this is not being demonstrated, what Ms. Korner is claiming, by this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we have your objection on the record, Mr. Krgovic. But for the reasons that -- underlying the admission of the previous document, this is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the -- I think the -- the problem is, again, the translation. Because the English translation says a truck of weaponry was handed over to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll let him read the sentence, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's okay, because the same word stands in Serbian both for "handed over" and to "surrender." And that is why I think it should be -- it should be given to the CLSS --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- perhaps for the retranslation. For --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't mind. We'll get that checked, Your Honours, and see. Right. Can we look now, please, at document P541, tab 8D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now this I don't imagine you've seen before either. It's a record of the Serbian minister of the interior, the Expert Board, held on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to page 2 in English, and I think the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "A meeting should be held --" do you see, under the -- under "Mr. Karisik," the -- became, you may or may not be aware, the leader of the special police. "A meeting should be held with the minister of the interior, the minister of defence, and General Kukanjac, about what has been done on the secret mobilization." Were you aware that even before an order was issued there was a mobilization going on of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner, but I can't see this particular paragraph in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see: "Milenko Karisik" on that page?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... and do you see it begins by saying "Mr. Karisik said ..."

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- all right. Did you know anything about this secret mobilization?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, could you look, please, moving on in time, to - all this happening in April - the next day in April, which is document, please, 1D531 at tab 9. Here we see -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1D -- thank you. 531.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 15th of April, the Serbian Republic declares a state of imminent threat of war and the formal mobilization of the TO in the whole territory of the Serbian Republic. "All conscripts are obliged to put themselves at the disposal of the municipal TO staffs in the Serbian Republic." And it's signed by Mr. Krajisnik. If we put this into context, on the 8th -- sorry. On the 5th of April, the Government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina orders a partial mobilization of the TO. On the 14th of April, the MUP is discussing the secret mobilization. And, on the 15th of April, there is the declaration of the imminent state of war and the order for mobilization. So do you agree that at that stage it would appear that roughly within days of each other both sides have decided there's clearly going to be a conflict, that is to say, the Muslims, and, I suppose, to a certain extent, the Croats, and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if we look at these dates, if I remember correctly, on the 15th of April the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was already established.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... no, it was -- you're absolutely right; it was -- there was an order - I'm sorry, we actually should have produced it - there was an order dated the very self-same day. So the Army of ABiH is formally then established. But, at the same time, the Serbs are also issuing it. And who came first may be a matter of discussion or argument. But the fact that it's both at the same time, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fact that, at the time, the Serbian people decided to remain within the federal republic. The then-TO, which was in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, started to disintegrate along ethnic lines, and I suppose that this decision was taken in order to have the remains of the TO properly organised and placed under the leadership of the Serbs, the then-Serbian leadership. As far as I know, nevertheless, the Serbian leadership continued to recognise the JNA and the TO as the only regular armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, what happened was that in the territories where the Serbs were in a majority, such as Celinac, or Banja Luka, I can't think of anywhere else at the moment, the TO was Serb. In other places, where there was less of an overall majority, the TO was divided, wasn't it, between the various ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the remains of the TO, as you call it, is not quite right, is it? It's simply that part of the TO was Serbian responded to the Serbian call for mobilization, and that part of the Muslim, where it was able to, responded to the president -- the Socialist Republic's call?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it's right, isn't it, that the majority of the weaponry that had been held by the TOs had been, in fact, back in 1991, collected, as a result of an order, by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that order, Ms. Korner. By doing so, the JNA tried to leave as little weaponry among the people as possible. However, I think that somebody should make a thorough analysis and to find out where all these weapons actually ended up. How many depots were captured, how many pieces of weapons were seized from these depots or from the JNA barracks that were under attack at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, if we look briefly, please, at the next document, because we see that decision by the Serbian Republic Assembly being put into effect, can you have a look, please, at document 1647. Tab 10, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, it's 1D170. Your Honours, I'm sorry. We discovered later it had been exhibited by the Defence. 1D170.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The following day, Mr. Subotic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you -- if we go to the second page in B/C/S and also in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he is putting into effect, by sending to the governments of the autonomous regions of the Serbian republic, and also to all Serbian municipality, order about an imminent state of war and to mobilise. Had you seen that before?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't you have received it yourself? Or not you personally, but at your command in Bihac. Or had you already moved by then?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. I was still in Bihac at the time, but I do not recall this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then, moving swiftly, I hope. Sift through this. Heading towards the end of April, and it was becoming clear, wasn't it, Colonel [sic], that the JNA was probably going to be pulled out?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there was enormous pressure, because I think that on the 6th of April Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by some members of the international community as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. All I'm asking, and I suppose one should say, was it clear to you as a serving officer in the JNA towards the end of April that it was likely that the JNA, as an army, would be pulled out of Bosnia? If you can't remember, or it wasn't, then say so now.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I remember clearly that period of insanity. We received an order towards the end of April to go to Sarajevo instead of Belgrade, and we just couldn't believe our eyes. Because we knew, or we supposed, and it turns out that we were right, that the war was going to take a totally different direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Actually, all I really wanted to know was whether it was clear to you that it was likely that the JNA would be pulled out of Bosnia at this period, end of April.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, there were hints of that being about to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can you have a look, please, at a document which is P550. Tab 12A. This is actually a report which I don't imagine you've looked at or -- or seen before. It came from a SNB agent in the CSB Banja Luka. It's dated the 27th of April. It starts by telling the reader that the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina has decided to form the TO. And there is a document to that effect, but we don't bother with it. And then it goes on to say this: "The Assembly took the view that the JNA must be prevented at any cost from withdrawing the equipment and ordnance from the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And that was right, wasn't it, General, that there was allegedly an order, although it was denied, from the socialist Bosnian -- socialist government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, saying that the JNA should be stopped and that was because they didn't want the JNA to take without it -- to leave with all the weapons. But, at the same time, the Serbs didn't want the JNA to leave either, did they? Because they wanted the weaponry and the people to stay in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember those developments, Ms. Korner. Although, I can't see here specifically whose doing the reporting or who put together the report itself. Nevertheless, I'm telling you that it was a minor chaos in terms of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there is, in fact, a report in a newspaper about that session, but I won't trouble you with it. Right. So that's -- so we've reached the end of April, and that's the situation. Now, have you ever had an opportunity of looking through the Mladic notebooks? Were you offered that opportunity by either of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll I'm going to ask you to have a look, please, at just a couple of entries for what was actually happening at the top level around this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, document P1753, which is at tab 4. And it's at page 210, both, I think, in English and B/C/S. If that's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 211 in English, please; and 214 in B/C/S, I'm told. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is General Mladic reporting -- sorry, recording, not reporting, apparently a meeting with General Adzic on the 30th of April of 1992, and he starts off by saying that: "The contents should not be made public and the contents of the talks should be disclosed to trustworthy brigade commanders."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the next page in B/C/S and English. Should be 211. It appears that Colonel Subotic, the minister of defence of the RS, was there. And he says: "This meeting has been organised because of BH. Nothing is organised there. I don't understand why the leadership of the RS didn't do anything except on the -- rely on the JNA staying in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We've proclaimed a TO of the Serbian Republic, and the army must remain in the territory ..." Now, I don't know, General, you may not be able to comment on this: Were you aware that the government at that stage, when it declared the TO, was relying on the JNA staying? If you're not able to comment, then say so.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I looked briefly at the previous document. I believe the last paragraph talks about the newly established TO continuing to be subordinated to the JNA as it existed at the time. As for the rest, I would refuse to comment. I agree with you on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, can I take you to another part which you may be able to assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 220 in both B/C/S and English. This is all part and parcel, it would appear, of the same meeting. On the 30th of April. Is that showing the right part? I don't think it is. It should be 220 in B/C/S. Yep. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "What next?" And then I suppose we should check who the speaker was there. Back some pages. Oh, this is General Adzic who speaks at length, it looks like. I'm sorry, and I'll give the reference if anybody wants to check it. That's what it appears. It starts page 213. "What next?" And he talks about the Presidency of the FRY. "If such a decision is taken, the government should invite all officers to defend their people. In order for this not to be chaotic, you will have to do the following ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think we need to go to the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Inform the commanders of brigades, regiments, and battalions to be on stand-by. At the given moment, they are to line up their forces and to do this. This is to be followed by a statement of the corps commander that the units are staying put." "2 JNA units are to pull out to areas inhabited by Serbs and replenish themselves 100 percent with Serbian soldiers and that the soldiers and officers will not abandon their people. "... mobilise to the maximum the Serbian TO forces and organise them in a military fashion --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the next page, please. Oh, no, it's at the bottom -- well, next page in English, please, but the same page in B/C/S at the bottom, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "... set the borders of the Serbian area in the territory of BH and fortify them." Now, do you agree, it's clear there that what General Adzic was saying is that the JNA, this All People's Army, would pull out into Serbian areas and replenish themselves with Serbian soldiers. That's obvious, actually. But what I want to know is -- don't answer that, General, because it's obvious. I'm just reading it. Did you receive an order --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Ms. Korner. I've been trying to say this all along. Let's try and be specific. These are serious things we're talking about. We don't have the JNA there. We have remnants of the JNA. The Slovene officers have already gone back to Slovenia. The Croats back to Croatia. The Muslims crossed over. Nevertheless, as I said at the outset, a small number of officers of other ethnicities still remained in the JNA. One didn't know where to go, where to take their families, where to put themselves up, where to find accommodation. There were all these logistical problems. It wasn't just about the JNA. It was very much about the JNA breaking at the seams literally, along ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but this is an order. Did you, as a Serb officer, receive an order to pull your units out, the JNA units, to Serb areas? You, the air force officer at that stage.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I, or, rather, my commander at the time, my commander received an order for us to move from Bihac to the Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I suppose that would be called a Serb area. But a Serb area in Bosnia. No?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question all right, but I thought you were asking me about my individual case and that of my commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... all right. Well, no. I know what -- we're going to come on to your individual case in a moment. But was your air force unit pulled out to Belgrade or was it sent somewhere to a Serb inhabited area in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as far as I know, as far as I remember, I was with the radar control units, where the radars were stationed at the time. You can't have a group of radar somewhere in a city or a town. At the time, we already had radars in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as far as I remember, at Kozara and on Mount Pljesevica. All of our equipment, taken over from the other units that were previously in Slovenia, was pulled out and taken to Serbia. That is, all of it that had not been looted and seized.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's move to the 5th of May, which is when the so-called order came from the federal republic to pull the JNA back to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look, please, at page 247, just for the date. This is just to establish the date. It's not clear what General Mladic is -- either it's questions to somebody or it's questions to him; I'm not sure which. But can we look, please, at page 248. Again, this is talks with General Adzic. And he's saying that the status of the army has failed -- the attempt to negotiate the status of the army with Mr. Izetbegovic has failed. And then, please, at 249. The next page, in B/C/S only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is leaving its army in the territory of BH to BH and it's calling on all three nations to reach agreement." What do you understand by that, General?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's difficult for me to interpret this. Firstly, because I don't see the part that you referred to. Based on the interpretation I receive, I am afraid it's not quite the same as stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, it should be the top of -- no, it's the -- yes, it's the top of the page that can you read. Can you read that out, please. The top of the page that you see there.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It has reached a level and that's as far as it got. Now we have no choice. The SRJ army --" now there's something that I can't figure out "... leaves B and H" - doesn't make sense - "and calls on all the three ethnicities to reach agreement."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one word here that I'm not quite able to make out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, does it, could it say -- well, sorry, that's just argument. We'll move on. Because if you go on down the page we see what General Adzic is saying: "We must not allow ourselves to fall apart in Bosnia-Herzegovina." "Us" being the Serbs, we -- we take it. "Take over the" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honours, I -- I really have to make one principal objection to this. I don't see how this, all of this, comes out of the -- the direct examination of this expert witness or from his particular expert report. I understand Ms. Korner is entitled to test his credibility, but, with all due respect, the -- the testing of the credibility cannot be done by reading the diary of the third person about the talks which he had with the fourth person and asking this witness to comment on that. And I sincerely believe there's absolutely no relevance in all of this, because all of his answers can -- can -- have the -- have the basis only on what he reads at the moment. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage, the General was present in Bosnia, operating as a member of the JNA. This is the 30th of April through to 5th of May. This part of -- this whole section of my cross-examination, and although I have no necessity to say why I'm doing it or to go beyond what is in his report, is actually based, both on his report and his evidence. In paragraph 50, he said, and maintains that is correct when I asked him about it, that the Serbian army was only formed as a result of the Muslim and Croatian armies being formed. And what I'm attempting, however incompetently, to show is that, in fact, the planning for the formation of the VRS, using the rump, or the JNA, had gone on for a great deal longer and was running at roughly the same time as the formation of the ABiH. Additionally, the General asserted that the VRS was made up only of the TO units. And I'll find the reference. This was in his evidence at page 23671. "General," he was asked at page -- at line 13, "please explain briefly of which units the army of the RS consisted and what is the essence of the VRS." And he said: "I already said, and I can repeat now, that on the 4th of May the federal leadership, and I mean that of Yugoslavia, adopted the decision on the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from BiH. After that, only TO units remained functional." And further on, Your Honours, we talked about the decisions. "The situation was the same in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ... that is, the army of the Serbian republic was made up exclusively of units and staffs of the Territorial Defence." And, Your Honours, what I'm showing, and I'm going to be showing further documents about that, is that is simply not the case. And, as I say, it is not meant as a criticism of the General. If the General had been shown the documents, he probably wouldn't have made a statement like that. But because he has, because he hasn't been shown the documents before, I've got to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I follow you, Ms. Korner. We're coming up on a break. But before we rise, coming back to this document that was admitted to replace 10296, the question, Ms. Korner, is whether 2389, which was assigned yesterday, whether that number needs to be vacated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I think it does. Otherwise, we really do get confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So ordered. Yesterday's number of 2389 is vacated. So we would return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to leave that entry because I'm told that there may be some mistranslations somewhere so I'm not going to waste any more time on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look at one last entry from the diary, and that's, please, first of all, at page 264 in English and B/C/S, I hope. It's page 260 in the full-typed version. Yep. 264. One page back. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just -- we see at the end this is still General Adzic going on, and it's not what I want to ask you about. But he's saying that -- or Mladic has recorded: "Invite for talks Colonel Milovanovic." That's the same Milovanovic, is it, who you quoted in your report, part of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the same person, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then we move to the 7th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I want to look at the next page, 265, please, in both -- it's the next page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this is talks which are being held between Mladic and other generals, because General Krstic, we saw, is there. And this is the vice-president of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Kostic, who says: "The decision to withdraw the citizens of the FRY, the Serbian people have not been abandoned to fend on its own. "For Serbs it's extremely important for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to be preserved. "Keep the materiel and technical equipment in the area. This is not a matter of us turning our backs on the Serbs in BH. We do not want to weaken the military population -- potential of the Serbian people." Would the vice-president of the SFRY be in a position to influence what the army did, as regards leaving materiel and equipment in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's difficult for me to answer that question. As far as I can tell by looking at this, these are certain political decisions that I was not entirely familiar with at the time. Nevertheless, I could give you a hand. I'm gradually beginning to understand what the problem appears to be. Your Honours, when I say "the problem," I mean the following: Thanks to Ms. Korner, who has provided me with Mr. Brown's report, if I remember correctly, there was a sentence there in that report that I noticed. The Army of the Republika Srpska was established based on the JNA. Reading Mr. Butler's report, I observed the following piece of phrasing: The VRS was established based on components of the JNA. And the third definition, Your Honours, you will find in my reports. I assert in my report that the VRS was established, based on the units and staffs of the TO. You have three expert witnesses with different assertions. Nonetheless, I base my own assertion on an official document, and, I repeat, a decision taken at the time by the then-assembly, and the decision reflects exactly what I say in my report. I also address the breakup of the JNA and the progress of this process. This is an exceptionally serious issue and requires a discussion that is structured in a totally different way. That would be the only way for us to arrive at a conclusion of what the JNA's role was at the time and what its tasks were. The only thing that we do know for sure is how it has gone down in history.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: General, thank you for that, and I'm glad that you found Mr. Brown's report illuminating. The point is this, that Mr. Brown and Mr. Butler, before they produced their reports, and particularly Mr. Brown, made a thorough study of all the documents that were available to them, and you didn't. And, as I said, I'm not blaming you for that. You didn't have access to them, and you weren't given them. But if you had seen all these documents, and there are more to come, wouldn't you be put in a position where you'd be prepared to agree that, in fact, the VRS was made up of large components of the JNA, assisted by the mobilization of the TO forces in Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I extremely respect Mr. Brown, but it's not up to me to assess Mr. Brown's and Mr. Butler's work. I stand by my statement. I come from this country, from the aforementioned Yugoslav People's Army. Both the country and the Yugoslav People's Army were in the process of disintegration. And you will have to admit that I'm pretty familiar with how the events took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, General, I regret to inform you - and after that we'll move back to the documents - that, I'm afraid, my suggestion is that, through no fault of your own, you do not have the knowledge that it was available certainly to Mr. Brown, because did you not study in depth, because you couldn't, the background documents and, in particular, those that relate to the 1st Krajina Corps. And that's my suggestion, so that it's clear, but I think you understand it. Now can we go back, please, to some of the other documents relating to this transformation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Please, could we look now at document -- sorry ... yes, 20 -- actually, I'm sorry. I am ... I'm going skip that one. You are familiar, are you, with the 12th of May Assembly, Mr. -- oh, sorry, now I've missed -- sorry -- with the 12th of May Assembly minutes? Actually, I'm sorry, I have missed one out. Well, firstly, can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I have seen it. I have noticed that this assembly session was mentioned in the analysis of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's the session that formally created -- or the decision that formally created the VRS. Are you saying you've not read the full minutes, including General Mladic's speech?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But I'd like you to look - and I'm sorry, that's the document I did miss by mistake - at document 13A, which is 20244, which is 7th of May. This is the 5th Corps, 5th Krajina Corps, sending to its units the telegram from the Federal Secretariat, which we can see relates to the 5th of May decision on the transformation of the JNA. "It has been ensured that members of the JNA who remain in the Republic of Bosnia ... or those being sent there will have the same rights as other members of the JNA. Accordingly, in order to ensure planned and organised implementation of this decision, all members of the JNA who have BH citizenship should be kept in their present posts in units and institutions in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So the order was that those of the JNA who were citizens of BiH should stay in their units in BiH; is that right? It's an actual order.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as far as I can see, this is not an order. This is just an option that is given to people to state their own opinion and position about this fact, and it is granted here that their entitlements and other rights will be regulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, so, you say the words "all members of the JNA who have BH citizenship should be kept in their present posts" offers you an option? Offers -- sorry, those with BH citizenship an option?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Ms. Korner, I remember from some specific examples that this was done according to the principle of voluntary decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were a JNA officer with Bosnian citizenship, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why didn't you stay in Bosnia instead of going to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I received an order upon which all officers had to act. It stipulated in great detail where I'm going to be transferred within the move to pull out the Yugoslav People's Army out. This order contained my establishment post and the garrison to which I am to be transferred. As a soldier, I obeyed this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, I'm sorry, General, but what you actually told the Court on the first day when Mr. Krgovic was asking you questions, at page 23635, was that you had gone -- this -- you even said it was in January that you wanted to sign up as an officer, that you wanted to present yourself to tell them what your credentials were. "They were supposed to send a request to my then-command within the JNA, where I served. "They didn't do that." Because: "The then-Serb leadership didn't ... have much confidence, didn't really trust me as an officer of the JNA." So apparently in January you tried. Did you make another attempt when this directive came out? Putting it at its lowest, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, Ms. Korner. But I was referring to the municipal leadership, not the leadership in general. Since they failed to invite me and, as a soldier, I received this order in the meantime, which was very precise, I had to abide by it. And I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, next at document, P1786. At tab 17, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report. And in paragraph 3 it talks about the deadline for the taking away of weapons which has expired and: "... the Banja Luka Ministry of Interior organs are making appropriate preparations to take away the weapons, people fear possible interethnic conflicts." Now, were you aware, and this is after you left, I agree, of the disarmament orders that were issued by the various municipal organs and regional organs?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't remember having seen this particular order, or, rather, this combat report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you had a rather interesting discussion with Mr. Cvijetic over disarmament with heavy -- people who had heavy weapons would be disarmed by the army, and people who had hunting rifles would be disarmed by the police. Can we take it on your side that, as you didn't really know from experience about disarmament, you were just agreeing with Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I've been sitting here for ten days now, and I don't have the transcript available to me on a daily basis so that I can check what was it that I talked on day 1 or day 2. Therefore, it is very difficult for me to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I accept that entirely, General. You don't have the advantage that we have. In summary form, and I'll turn up the page of the transcript if necessary, Mr. Cvijetic put to you that where there was disarmament going on and the persons to be disarmed had big weaponry, such as mortars and the like, it would be the army who did it; whereas, if they had hunting rifles, it would be the police that did it. Are you able to say one way or another, except from, I suppose, common sense points of view, and depending on the armament, what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't know who did what in any specific case. One should have to look at a specific order which probably gives instructions as to who is supposed to do what.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Thank you, sir. And that's, rather, what I thought. I just wanted to look at paragraph 6, though, which is more on the topic that we've dealing with at the moment. "Soldiers from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia are arriving at the corps unit [sic] according to plan." So would you accept that it's clear that people with Bosnian -- who were Bosnian Serbs were coming from the FRY to re-enforce the corps, the 1st Krajina Corps, as it then was?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, at the time, surely there were elements of JNA units that remained in Serbia, that there were people who were born or had the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think that this refers to these people when you cited this order and what was offered to them, but, as I said, I don't remember that being an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, in fact, you may well believe it's not an order in the same way because it says, it continues: "Officers are still dissatisfied over having to declare whether they wish to be in" - effectively - "Serbia or the Serbian Republic of BH ..." So I accept you may well be right that it wasn't an order in the way that I suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, next can we look, please, at document number 19, which is tab 19, 20220.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the first -- or it's still calling itself the 5th Corps then. Probably still was, as we'll see. 18th of May. Dealing with conscripts. "All military conscripts who've been called up shall be admitted into all the units of the 5th Corps. Special attention shall be devoted to the admission of other nationalities (Muslims, Croats, and others)." And then the distribution list of this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go, please, to the second page in B/C/S and second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the distribution -- the order, I think, is actually signed by General Talic, I believe. And then it's to all units, is that right, or to the units that were subordinated?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And I think we dealt with this yesterday, but just to reinforce. An order such as this, which has an effect on units which are subordinated, should be sent to all those units. A list of those units should occur. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, Ms. Korner. Provided the contents of the order pertains to all the units. It sometimes happened that some contents, some orders, could be sent only to specific units; whereas, the others are supposed to be sent to all units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Then we're nearly at the end of this section.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we move, please, to document -- yes. 23 -- sorry. 22 ... actually ... yes. 23, which is 20231.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the reason I'm going to deal with this next series of documents, General, is at one stage when you were shown the order -- sorry, the decision which constituted the VRS, you said there was a long gap between the 12th of May and I believe it was the 18th of -- 26th of June -- 18th of June, when the formal order -- the formal VRS order came out. And I want to show you perhaps why it took a little bit of time. 26th of May, this is a document that has been written by, as he has then become, Major-General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page both in English and B/C/S, please. So that's now Major-General Milovanovic. And if we go back to the first page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's headed "Army of the Main Staff of the Serbian Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina," 26th of May, to the commander, (Chief of Staff). "At the meeting on the 26th of May, 1992, the commanders and the Chief of Staff of the army of the Serbian Republic of BH and the top political leadership ... discussed possible options for the Serbian Republic Army of organisational and establishment structure. It was concluded, amongst [sic] other things, that it should be an army consisting of quick, mobile, and efficient units based on current establishment formations, existing combat hardware, weapons, and other military equipment. Light infantry brigades are to be the preferred option, while infantry brigades should be formed ..." Going over the -- leaving aside various discussions there, going over the page again, at the top: "It was also agreed that our army should be equipped for an offensive defence and for guarding the Serbian territories in BH, not to conquer territory belonging to the others." And then it's signed by him. And the distribution is to the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija, Eastern Bosnia, and Herzegovina Corps. You relied for part of your report on something that General Milovanovic had testified about in the Perisic [sic] case. Were you also aware that he had testified about how he came to be in the VRS? Were you shown that part? Did you read the whole transcript?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you put in as part of the Defence documents was that part of the transcript that you relied on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have up, please, document, which has been given the 65 ter 20233.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was just -- luckily for us, Ms. Deirdre Montgomery was in Perisic case. Milovanovic never testified in Perisic case. Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, did I say Perisic? Sorry. Popovic. Sorry, Your Honours, that was a ... it was Popovic. And it's footnoted in the General's report, part of the transcript. But I'd like to look at another part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'd like you to look at another part, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at page 12151. Page 21 in e-court. He was asked by Mr. McCloskey how his position evolved during those events. And he said, and I'm going to summarize, that General --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I don't have the document in front of me. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do. But you can't -- well, you may be able to read some of it in English, but I'm afraid there's no -- as far as I'm aware, there's no B/C/S transcript of this. Unless the Defence have got a copy. How did you -- well, never mind. Let me summarize what is said here, and let me ask you if you know this. That on the 11th of May, General Kukanjac was removed from the position of the commander of the 2nd Army to be replaced by General Mladic. First, did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that event, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And General Milovanovic said he was appointed as chief of the 2nd Army. And he wanted to know why he was being sent to Bosnia, knowing that the JNA was in the process of withdrawal and it was disappearing from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he was told to go to Han Pijesak, to report to General Mladic, who was supposed to brief him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he said he got there on the 11th of May, waiting for Mladic, and he found 12 people, Mladic, Gvero, including four generals. Then General Mladic briefed us and he told us that the 2nd army was being transformed, that the following day the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Banja Luka would make a decision on the establishment of the Army of the Republika Srpska and that we had been appointed as members of the Main Staff. Mladic would be its commander, I would be its chief, General Gvero would be assistant commander for moral guidance. Djukic, assistant commander. And so on and so forth. Now, what General Milovanovic was saying there, and I don't know whether you can confirm it or not, was that the whole of the -- effectively, the 2nd Military District was being transformed into the VRS. Now, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm not sure that it can be interpreted in this way. Although, I find it very difficult without closely studying the transcript in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you were -- either you were -- how did you get the transcript that you relied on? Was that something given to you by the Defence, or did you have the transcript? Because you only had -- you only referred to a few pages of that testimony.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. As far as I remember, I only referred to the portion in relation to General Milovanovic saying that the armies being created were applying the rules and regulations of the former JNA. Again, if I remember correctly. I do believe that I got the document from Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, if Mr. Krgovic has the full transcript, which he may have because he was in the case, you can have a look at it if you require to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we look then, please - and, as I say, this is near the end of what I want to do on this topic - at a document number 01651. At tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The following day, in response to General Milovanovic's request, the 1st Krajina Corps replies, giving its proposal for the organisation of the 1st Krajina Corps. Have you -- no, I don't imagine you've seen this document before either.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's not on my list --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ...

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- then I haven't, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In which case, I don't think I can ask you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But can we then move, please, to the 1st of June. And it's document number L51. Oh, and it's at tab 30. Four days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Law on the Army is published, 1st of June. And under Article -- as you say, the Army of the Serbian Republic, I think you dealt with that, so you looked at a different document, is the armed force of the Serbian Republic of Herzegovina. [As read] "Article 3, the persons serving in the army are soldiers and employees of the army. Pursuant to the present law, the following shall be members of the army, soldiers, cadets of Military Academies (herein after cadets), active members of the military reserve personnel whilst on military duty in the army. Active member of the military shall include officers, non-commissioned officers, and soldiers under contract." And I take it that you are familiar with that, because you looked at it with Mr. Krgovic, I believe. Is that right, General? I'm sorry, I need an answer. You're familiar with the law?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I believe that document is actually on my list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, exactly. So the answer is yes. All right. Can we just look at Article 9 for a moment, which is the next page, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the same page in B/C/S, but the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Replenishment -- it's headed "Replenishment of the Army." Article 8: "Citizens ... shall join the army pursuant to regulations issued by competent bodies ... based on conscription or the regulation on the admission to activity military service, i.e., to cadet school." Article 9: [As read] "Military units and institutions shall be replenished with troops from the active forces, reserves, materiel, et cetera. In a state of war, imminent threat of war, or in a state of emergency, the army may be replenished with volunteers. Pursuant to provisions of paragraph 2 herein, volunteers are persons joining the army at their own request, without a war time assignment, and the persons described in paragraph 2 herein shall have equal rights and duties to members of the military, i.e., conscripts." Now, do you agree - and you are familiar with this whole law - that nowhere is there a mention of resubordinated police being members of the army, either as conscripts or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, in my opinion, one should establish a link between this law, the Law on Military Duty of the former state, and the Law on All People's Defence, which we discussed and which envisages the involvement of military police in combat operations. Only then could we properly discuss the subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... no, I appreciate what you're trying to say and what you've been trying to say throughout your evidence on this issue, but at the moment it really is a simple question: Is there any mention in the Law on the Military, passed on 1st of June, 1992, of resubordinated police, under Article 104 of the All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we would need to go through every single article of this law. It is possible that it is not mentioned in this law. I do, however, assert that there are provisions in other laws saying that from battalion commander level up, in a situation of war or imminent threat of war, may resubordinate someone from the police. The law entitles that commander to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, two things: You have overnight to consider it. I would be grateful if you would point me to any law or regulation that says in times of imminent threat of war a commander may -- a brigade commander, or officers to the level of a brigade commander, may resubordinate police, other than Article 104 of the All People's Defence. I'll give you overnight. But, anyhow, that's the only question I want to ask you about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look now, please, at document 1D534, MFI, apparently. Not sure why. Just a second. Ah, yes, well, in fact, this was a document - [indiscernible] - that Mr. Zecevic attempted to put in and Mr. Hannis -- I'm not sure ... and Mr. Hannis pointed out that there was a military expert to whom it could be put, but nobody seems to have bothered to put it to him. So I'm quite happy to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the decision of the 15th of June, 1992, on the forming, organisation, establishment, command, and control of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, have you seen that document before? I don't think that's on your list at all. In fact, I know it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm told it was Mr. Bajagic, that this was the attempt to put it through.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that document at all?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, this document is on my list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, General. I may have missed it. Can you tell us where you footnoted it? In any event, so you are familiar with it. Let's not waste time. I accept it entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In which case, Your Honours, Mr. Hannis objected to it going in through Mr. Bajagic. But Mr. Zecevic certainly wants it in. We're happy to have it in as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Ms. Korner. I don't have any objection. Document should be de-MFI'd, actually, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. So ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. In which case it must be in the Defence documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, then, on this -- as I say, the document that you were shown by the Defence for the 18th of June, which is tab 11 in their bundle, is -- it's got the 65 ter number 39D2. And there's the decision that you were shown by Mr. Krgovic. Now, General, the reason that I've been taking you through, somewhat torturously and at length, all these documents, apart from whether or not the TO formed the bulk of the VRS, is because you told Mr. Krgovic that you couldn't understand why there was this gap between the 12th of May -- I better find the exact reference. Yes, it's 23676, second day of your testimony: "General," it was asked of you, "can you tell us what implication ... this order has [sic] in the process of ... forming of an army?" And you said: "It is slightly unusual that nearly a month elapsed after the decision that we mentioned a minute ago to establish an army. And then one month later, an order is issued to form unit commands of the ... Serbian Republic ..." In fact, as we can see, there was pretty much continuous activity, wasn't there, between the 12th of May and the 18th of June when this all -- 15th of June, when this order came out. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I accept that certain consultations were underway. We see the Main Staff sending suggestions to the corps and the corps sending their own suggestions back. All I did was voice my opinion, as it is. In a war situation, the process should have been a lot speedier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the thing was you voiced your opinion on -- without the knowledge, didn't you? You hadn't seen the documents that I've just shown you. With the exception of the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if you look at my list, item 28 specifically, it reads: "Decision of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on establishing, forming, organising and commanding the VRS."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. You misunderstand. What you hadn't seen was the Milovanovic order asking for suggestions; the 1 KK reply, and presumably all the other corps replied as well; the earlier discussions, about which we can see in the Mladic diary; and -- and the like. You hadn't looked at any of that, had you? And that's why you said, Well, it's rather odd that it should take nearly a month.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Ms. Korner. I was wondering as an officer, as a soldier, given the conditions of war and the 12th of May Assembly decision about all this thing about the army being set up, my personal opinion is this should have been a lot speedier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I regret to say, I think for the rest of this afternoon, I want to return to the controversial issue of resubordination. Now, General, it really comes down to -- to three or four things, doesn't it? First, how does resubordination come about?
